title: Knowing yourself
hookLine: knowing others is wisdom, knowing yourself is enlightenment; who knows they have enough is rich (Tao Te Ching 33)

lines: A STRANGER'S FACE, OR YOUR OWN SNAP?
ONE OUTWARD, ONE BACK AT YOU.
cards: A woman on a morning train watches the man across the aisle. Tight jaw, a glance at his phone, a sigh. In ten seconds she has a whole story about his day.
An hour earlier she snapped at her brother over nothing, and that one came with a ready excuse attached, an excuse about him.

Chapter thirty-three of the Tao Te Ching is short, and it's built in pairs: two kinds of knowing, two kinds of strength, two kinds of wealth. In each pair, one half points outward and the other points back at you.

teach.b: First, knowing. In James Legge's translation the chapter opens: "He who knows other men is discerning; he who knows himself is intelligent." Discerning is no small thing.
Reading people is a real skill. But the chapter sets a second kind of knowing beside it, and the Chinese word there means bright, or clear. Seeing yourself is a kind of light.
Whoever overcomes others is strong, the chapter says, and whoever overcomes themselves is mighty. Winning a fight takes muscle. Not starting the fight you were itching for takes something more.

You may remember this one from day thirteen of this path: whoever is content with what they have is rich. And whoever keeps going with steady effort, the chapter adds, has a firm will. It doesn't say stop trying.
It holds enough and effort together. The rich person here isn't the one with the most; it's the one who can tell when there's enough. Fourth, the ending, which is a riddle.
Whoever doesn't lose their place endures, it says, and whoever dies but doesn't perish has long life.

teach.h: HE WHO KNOWS HIMSELF IS INTELLIGENT.
teach.b: Readers have heard different things in that line, and the chapter doesn't explain it. So, back on the train. The outward half of each pair is about other people: reading them, beating them, getting more than them.
Chapter thirty-three keeps turning the mirror around. Knowing yourself, here, is catching the excuse before it finishes forming, and asking what in you just reacted.

how: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often use chapter thirty-three as a prompt for self-examination: noticing their own reactions, mastering themselves rather than others, and learning to recognize enough.

o: judging others so you can feel more secure
seeing yourself clearly, a kind of inner light
knowing which people you can trust

s: chapter thirty-three says knowing other people is worthless
it calls knowing others discerning; it sets knowing yourself beside it as a clearer kind of light.
the chapter says whoever is content with what they have is rich
and it pairs that with steady effort, which shows a firm will.
the chapter tells readers to stop trying once they have enough
it holds both together: content is rich, and steady effort is a firm will.

games.q: two people. one can read everyone in the room. the other knows why they themselves do what they do. how does chapter thirty-three describe them?
o: the first is wise; the second is selfish.
the first is discerning; the second is intelligent.
games.why: Legge: "he who knows other men is discerning; he who knows himself is intelligent." the chapter honors both, and turns the mirror around in the second.

practice: Go back over the last day and find one moment when you reacted: irritation, a quick yes you didn't mean, a sudden urge to leave. Don't judge it or explain it away; just ask quietly, what was that, in me?
If an answer comes, keep it; if nothing does, the asking is enough.

wordCard.voice: Knowing yourself. Chapter thirty-three sets it beside knowing others: knowing others is discerning, and knowing yourself, it says, is clear and bright. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese: bright, clear; the word chapter thirty-three uses for knowing yourself, which Legge renders intelligent.

carryVoice: Your line: know myself. The mirror turns back before it points out. See you tomorrow.
